title: [News] U.S. Tightens AI Chip Export Rules: What the Changes Mean for TSMC, ASE, and Taiwan’s AI Supply Chain
html:
The U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has tightened restrictions on AI chips and overseas computing access, raising concerns about potential disruptions to semiconductor supply chains. According to Commercial Times, the new rules could affect Taiwanese manufacturers across foundry, packaging, and AI server supply chains, although the extent of the impact remains uncertain.

TSMC, Samsung Foundry, and OSAT Providers Face Tighter Compliance Requirements

Among the key changes, the new rules narrow export license exemptions for foundries and outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) providers, according to Central News Agency. Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs (MOEA) explains that Taiwanese semiconductor and AI server manufacturers primarily operate on a contract manufacturing basis, with U.S. customers responsible for applying to BIS for necessary licenses when their orders involve restricted products, the report adds.

In response, TSMC said it is reviewing the new regulations and will comply with all applicable laws and regulations, according to Commercial Times.

TechNews suggests that major foundry and packaging providers, including TSMC, Samsung, ASE, and Amkor, could face stricter customer verification requirements, potentially delaying orders from Chinese chip designers pending U.S. export approvals. However, the immediate operational impact could remain limited, as tight advanced-node capacity may allow other international customers to fill production slots freed up by delayed Chinese orders, while advanced AI packaging capacity remains fully utilized.

Commercial Times also reports that Taiwanese manufacturers specializing in mature and specialty processes expect relatively limited direct exposure, as the restrictions primarily target advanced computing chips. Packaging suppliers, meanwhile, anticipate greater scrutiny of customer backgrounds and end uses, potentially requiring stricter contractual declarations, customer checks, and shipment controls.

Taiwanese AI Suppliers Monitor Orders as 2027 Visibility Weakens

Beyond foundries and packaging, the restrictions could also affect Taiwan’s broader AI supply chain. According to Commercial Times, component suppliers believe Taiwanese manufacturers could continue securing orders regardless of shifts in demand between NVIDIA GPUs and cloud providers’ custom ASICs. While orders for 1H27 are largely secured, visibility for 2H27 remains uncertain, with customer deployment plans and delivery schedules remaining key factors to watch.

The potential impact varies across Taiwan’s AI component supply chain. Commercial Times reports that memory suppliers are watching whether prolonged export license reviews could delay data center projects and slow procurement. Optical communications suppliers, meanwhile, warn that postponed overseas AI cluster deployments could push back demand for high-speed optical modules and related components. Thermal management suppliers see a different implication: with AI supply chain capacity still tight, project delays could provide some relief from existing capacity constraints.

U.S. Curbs Could Reshape Taiwan’s AI Server Orders in Southeast Asia

The potential impact extends to overseas AI infrastructure deployments, particularly in Southeast Asia. According to TrendForce, the new restrictions could raise chip procurement barriers, with Taiwan’s AI server shipments to the region expected to become increasingly concentrated among U.S. cloud service providers (CSPs). Orders from non-U.S. customers could face longer approval times and higher compliance costs.

Over the longer term, TrendForce expects the restrictions to constrain China’s access to computing resources, potentially making AI model training more challenging and shifting greater focus toward inference. Chinese CSPs may increase demand for domestic AI chips, in-house ASICs, and legally importable NVIDIA products such as the RTX PRO 5500, although supply bottlenecks could limit availability. The U.S. and China may also negotiate over the new rules, leaving their ultimate impact uncertain.
